967.title: Mother Teresa
967.hook: a nun in a white sari kneels on a Calcutta pavement beside a dying stranger
967.howItsDone: The Missionaries of Charity run homes for the dying, the sick and abandoned children, and volunteers of any faith or none often help with washing, feeding and simply sitting with residents. Catholics keep her feast as Saint Teresa of Calcutta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Oscar Romero, an archbishop who said from the pulpit what was being done to the poor. Your line: the voice of the voiceless.

A man is lying on a pavement in Calcutta, the city now called Kolkata. People step around him. A small woman in a white cotton sari with blue edges stops, kneels, and touches his face. She and another sister carry him to a long room near a temple, with low cots in rows. They wash him. They give him something to drink. They ask his name. If he dies tonight, he'll die clean, with someone beside him who knows what he's called. The world came to know that woman as Mother Teresa.

She was born Agnes, to an Albanian family in the Balkans, and became a nun with the Sisters of Loreto, teaching girls in a convent school in Calcutta. Outside the school walls was another city: people sleeping, sick and dying in the streets. She later described a call within her call: to leave the convent and live among the poorest people she could find. With her bishop's and the Church's permission, she did, and the community she started became the Missionaries of Charity. Underneath it all is a verse in Matthew. Jesus describes the Son of man coming in glory to judge the nations, and the king tells people they fed him, clothed him, visited him. They're baffled: when? The answer, in the King James Bible: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." She took that literally. She taught her sisters that the dying man on the pavement was Jesus, in what she called a distressing disguise. So the work wasn't, for her, social service with prayer added. It was the prayer. Now the honest part: she has admirers and critics. Some doctors and journalists questioned the medical care in her homes and how donations were used. And after her death, her private letters were published, showing that for long stretches she felt God was absent, a darkness she told almost no one about, while she kept getting up and going back to the cots. Catholics now honor her as Saint Teresa of Calcutta.

Think of someone who is ill, or old, or alone a lot of the time: a neighbor, a grandparent, someone in a hospital bed, someone who eats by themselves. See their face clearly and stay with them a while, the way a sister stays by a cot, without fixing anything. If you pray, hold them before God by name.
Mother Teresa. A nun who left her convent school to care for the dying and the abandoned, and who saw Jesus in each of them.
Your line: do it for him. Unto one of the least of these. Nine hundred sixty-seven days, and counting.

968.title: Janani Luwum
968.hook: a Ugandan archbishop puts his name to a letter against Idi Amin's killings, and is killed
968.howItsDone: The Church of Uganda and other Anglican churches commemorate Janani Luwum as a martyr, and in Uganda his day is marked with services, especially in the north where he was born. His statue is among the modern martyrs above the west door of Westminster Abbey.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mother Teresa, kneeling beside a man nobody else stopped for. Your line: do it for him.

People are disappearing in Uganda. Neighbors taken at night and never seen again. Fear in the towns. In Kampala, the capital, the country's Anglican bishops write a letter to the president, Idi Amin. It's polite, and it's terrifying, because it puts in writing what people have been afraid to say aloud. One of the names on it is the archbishop's. He knows what happens to people who put their names to things like this. He signs anyway.

His name was Janani Luwum. He grew up in northern Uganda, and as a young man he was caught up in the East African Revival, a movement of Christians who met in small groups, confessed their sins to one another out loud, and called each other brother and sister across tribe and class. That habit of plain speaking stayed with him. As archbishop of the Church of Uganda, he went to see Amin in person to raise the cases of people who had vanished. After the bishops' letter, he was summoned, accused of plotting, and paraded before soldiers and officials. Then he was taken away. The government announced he had died in a car accident. The church didn't accept that story, and remembers him as a martyr, killed for what he said. The Greek word behind martyr is the same word the King James Bible renders witnesses in Acts, where Jesus tells his followers: "ye shall be witnesses unto me." And in Revelation the same word is used of a man who was killed: "Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you." A witness, and one who dies for the witness. Luwum is both. A line from Jesus speaks to that kind of moment: "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul." It's not a promise that nothing bad will happen. It's a claim about what fear is allowed to decide. Today his statue stands above the great west door of Westminster Abbey in London, among other modern martyrs. And in Uganda, his day is kept.
screen: `FEAR NOT THEM WHICH KILL THE BODY.`

Then think of anyone there who is afraid tonight, of a government, a gun or a hunger. If you pray, pray for them and for those who still speak up when it's costly; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with care.
Janani Luwum. Archbishop of Uganda, who confronted Idi Amin about the killings and was killed himself. A martyr, and a witness.
Your line: courage in kampala. A witness, to the end. Day nine hundred sixty-eight, done.

969.title: Solidarity
969.hook: in Poland, striking workers kneel for Mass at the shipyard gate, and faith and a trade union help bring peaceful change
969.howItsDone: In Catholic teaching, solidarity is one of the principles of social teaching, and Catholics pray for workers on the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker. Catholics honor Jerzy Popiełuszko as a martyr, and his grave in Warsaw is visited by pilgrims.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janani Luwum, an archbishop who signed the letter and raised the killings with the president himself. Your line: courage in kampala.

The gate of a shipyard in Gdańsk, on the Polish coast, is covered in flowers. Someone has hung a picture of the pope on it, and a wooden cross. Inside, the workers are on strike. Outside, a priest sets up an altar, and the strikers kneel on the concrete for Mass. Others line up for confession on folding chairs by the fence. The government is communist, wary of the church, and watching. The workers want a union of their own, free of the party, and they paint its name on their banners.

The union was called Solidarność, Solidarity, and an electrician named Lech Wałęsa became its face. It was a trade union, not a church, and its members included believers and nonbelievers. But in Poland the Catholic Church was a large institution the state didn't control, and the two leaned on each other. The pope was Polish: John Paul the Second. At the start of his time as pope, he told the crowds, in effect, do not be afraid. Jesus says it in the Gospels. When the disciples see him walking on the water, terrified, the King James Bible has him say: "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid." Before the strikes, when the pope came home to Poland, crowds gathered in the open for his Masses. Then the crackdown came. Martial law. Solidarity banned. Leaders jailed. In Warsaw a young priest, Jerzy Popiełuszko, said Masses for the homeland, packed with workers, and kept repeating Paul's line to the Romans: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." Secret police officers abducted and killed him. His grave became a place of pilgrimage. And still the movement didn't turn to violence. Years later, the government sat down at a round table with Solidarity and agreed to partly free elections, and Solidarity won almost every seat it was allowed to contest. Solidarity is also a word in Christian teaching: people are bound up with one another, so another's burden is partly yours. Paul says it plainly: "Bear ye one another's burdens."

Start with what's around you, the chair, the light, your clothes, your next meal: somebody built, wired, sewed, grew, drove or cleaned for each. Picture a few of those workers, a night shift, a warehouse, a field, a shipyard, and let one of their burdens sit with you a moment. If you pray, pray for workers by name or by trade; if you don't, let the thanks be enough.
Solidarity. The Polish trade union that grew alongside the church and helped bring peaceful change. And an old idea: your neighbor's burden is partly yours.
Your line: be not afraid. In the end, a round table, not a war. Until tomorrow.

970.title: Desmond Tutu
970.hook: a South African archbishop who preached against apartheid, then listened to the truth told at the Truth and Reconciliation Commission
970.howItsDone: Anglicans remember Desmond Tutu, and his writing on ubuntu, forgiveness and reconciliation is read in churches, schools and peace work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Solidarity, workers kneeling for Mass at a shipyard gate in Poland. Your line: be not afraid.

What does the person in charge do when the testimony is too much to bear? A hall in South Africa: rows of chairs, microphones, headphones for translation. A witness describes what was done to him in a police cell long before, and what it did to his family. At the long table facing him sits a small man in a bishop's purple shirt. Partway through, he puts his head down on the table and weeps, in front of everyone. Then he lifts his head, and the hearing goes on. He chaired those hearings, and he insisted on hearing everything.

Desmond Tutu was an Anglican priest who became archbishop of Cape Town. Under apartheid, the system that separated South Africans by race and kept power in white hands, he preached that it was a sin, not just a bad policy, because every person is made in the image of God. He marched, he buried the dead after massacres, he called on the world to put pressure on the government, and he laughed a great deal. When apartheid ended, the new president, Nelson Mandela, asked him to chair the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The idea was unusual. Victims would tell their stories in public, and be heard. People who had committed political crimes could ask for amnesty, but only if they told the whole truth about what they had done. Truth first. Then, maybe, reconciliation. Tutu drew on the Bible for both halves. Jesus says, in the King James Bible, "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." And Paul writes that God "hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation." Tutu often spoke of ubuntu, a southern African idea he explained as: a person becomes a person through other people. In his telling, if you dehumanize someone, you lose some of your own humanity too. Forgiveness, he was clear, didn't mean forgetting, or pretending it wasn't so bad; forgiving starts with naming what was done. Not everyone agreed with the commission. Some families felt amnesty let the people who killed their loved ones walk away, and they said so. Tutu listened to that too. He called the work unfinished.

Bring to mind someone you're out of step with, a friend, a sibling, a parent, a colleague, and instead of rehearsing the argument, look for one plain true sentence about your own part: I was short with you, or I didn't call. Hold it, and if you pray, bring that sentence and that person before God; if not, just keep the sentence.
Desmond Tutu. The archbishop who called apartheid a sin, and then chaired a commission built on telling the truth before seeking reconciliation.
Your line: truth, then reconciliation. Forgiving isn't the same as forgetting. That's day nine hundred seventy.

971.title: Survival under Soviet rule
971.hook: while churches were shut, grandmothers kept faith alive in hidden prayer until churches reopened
971.howItsDone: Orthodox homes may keep an icon corner with a lamp, and in some families grandparents teach children the prayers and the sign of the cross. Russian and other Orthodox churches now honor the new martyrs and confessors who suffered under Soviet rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Desmond Tutu, weeping at the table, then lifting his head to keep listening. Your line: truth, then reconciliation.

Don't tell your teacher. A grandmother says it softly, with a child on her knee, in a small apartment high in a gray block. In the corner, up where two walls meet, there's a little shelf with a painted icon and a tiny oil lamp. She has just taught the child to touch forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other, and to repeat a prayer after her, line by line. Don't tell anyone at school. The child nods, not really knowing why. This is how faith got through the years when the state wanted it gone.

In the Soviet Union, the state taught that religion would fade away, and it worked hard to help it fade. Churches were closed, and some were turned into warehouses, clubs or museums of atheism. Priests and bishops were arrested; some were shot, some sent to camps. Believers could lose a job or a place at university. And not only the Orthodox: Catholics, Lutherans and Baptists were pressed too, and so were Muslims and Jews. So who kept the faith alive? In many stories from those years, the grandmothers, the babushkas. Some say officials paid less attention to old women in headscarves. They had less to lose, and some were raising the children while the parents worked. They kept the icon corner. They baked the Easter bread. They taught the prayers in whispers. Some family stories tell of grandmothers quietly taking a baby to a priest to be baptized, without telling the parents. The Bible has this pattern too. A letter in Paul's name to his young friend Timothy remembers, in the King James Bible, "the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice." Faith passed down a kitchen, not a lecture hall. When the Soviet system fell and churches reopened, grandmothers were among those standing inside, some in the same headscarves. Some of the young people who came in after them had first learned to cross themselves on a babushka's knee. The state had the schools, the newspapers and the police. The grandmothers had the corner shelf, and patience.

Bring to mind a grandmother, yours or someone else's, or any older person who passed something on to you: a recipe, a song, a prayer, a way of folding laundry, or of not giving up. Picture her hands doing it, and notice what of hers you still carry without thinking. Living or not, hold her with gratitude, and if you pray, thank God for her by name.
Icon. A painted image kept on a corner shelf, the thing grandmothers quietly guarded through the years when churches were shut and believers pressed.
Your line: the babushkas kept it. Lois, then Eunice, then Timothy. Day nine hundred seventy-one, done.

972.title: Candles in Leipzig (1989)
972.hook: Monday prayers for peace in St. Nicholas Church become peaceful marches with candles, and soon the Wall is open
972.howItsDone: St. Nicholas Church in Leipzig still holds Monday prayers for peace. In churches of several traditions, Christians light candles as a sign of prayer, including prayer for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an icon on a corner shelf, and a prayer whispered on a grandmother's knee. Your line: the babushkas kept it.

Monday evening in the East German city of Leipzig. Outside St. Nicholas Church, a sign says the church is open to all. Inside, the pews fill. Some people come every week to pray for peace. Some haven't been inside a church in their lives, and come because it's one of the few rooms in town where people say out loud what they think. A pastor reads, people pray, someone speaks about the country. Then the doors open, the crowd steps out into the dark square, and many of them are holding lit candles.

East Germany was a communist state that watched its people closely. The churches were tolerated, barely, and became a kind of shelter for honest talk. In Leipzig, St. Nicholas held prayers for peace every Monday, and its pastor, Christian Führer, kept the doors open to anyone: believers, doubters, people who wanted to leave the country, people who wanted to change it. Church peace groups wore a badge of a man beating a sword into a plow, a line found in the prophets Isaiah and Micah. In the King James Bible: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks." Then the prayers spilled into the streets. After the service, people walked the ring road around the city center, more of them as the weeks went on, holding candles and calling out: no violence, and, we are the people. Here's the detail people in Leipzig tell. If you carry a candle in the open air, you need one hand to hold it and the other to shield the flame. That leaves no hand free for a stone. On one Monday that autumn, soldiers and police were ready, and people feared shooting. It didn't come. Not long after, the Berlin Wall opened. A remark often credited to an East German leader puts it plainly: they were prepared for everything, except candles and prayers. Historians name other causes for the fall: the economy, Moscow's changes, a border opening elsewhere. The prayers weren't the whole story. But they were in it, and so were Jesus's words: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."
screen: `ONE HAND FOR THE CANDLE, ONE TO SHIELD.`

segments.voice: If you can light a candle safely, do; if not, a lamp or a phone's light will do. Cup your hands around it, the way they did in Leipzig, and notice that your hands are full. Then hold one place, near or far, where people need peace tonight, and if you pray, pray for it.
Peacemakers. Leipzig's Monday prayers for peace that became candlelit marches with no violence, part of how the wall came down.
Your line: candles and prayers. Hands too full to hold a stone. See you tomorrow.

973.title: Rwanda (1994)
973.hook: in a country full of churches, genocide happened even inside them; the work of reconciliation goes on
973.howItsDone: Churches in Rwanda hold services during the national period of remembrance, keep some church buildings as genocide memorials, and run reconciliation groups where survivors and perpetrators meet.

segments.voice: Yesterday: peacemakers, hands too full for stones. Your line: candles and prayers. This week brought a nun, an archbishop, a union, a commission, grandmothers and candles. It ends with a harder story.

A brick church in a Rwandan village. Inside, on the long benches, there are no people. There are clothes. Piles of them, faded shirts and dresses and small sweaters, left where they were found. The church is a memorial now. People ran to it because a church was supposed to be safe. It wasn't. This lesson is heavy, and it's fine to pause it and come back. Today: what happened in the churches, and what Christians there are still doing about it.
screen: `A CHURCH WAS SUPPOSED TO BE SAFE.`

segments.voice: Rwanda is a small, green, hilly country in east-central Africa, and church was part of ordinary life there: Catholic, Anglican, Adventist, Pentecostal. Then came the genocide against the Tutsi. Neighbors killed neighbors, urged on by radio, with machetes and guns. Hutu who refused or who hid people were killed too. Tutsi families fled to churches, as they had in earlier troubles, and in some of those churches they were massacred. The honest part has to be said plainly. Some clergy and church workers took part, or handed people over, or stayed silent, and some were later tried and convicted. Some historians trace how colonial rulers and missionaries had hardened the line between Hutu and Tutsi long before. And some priests, nuns, pastors and ordinary believers hid people in their homes and ceilings, and some died for it. Both are true. The Bible has words for both. When Cain kills his brother, God says in the King James Bible: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground." And the first letter of John: "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar." Afterward, Rwandan church leaders asked forgiveness, and so did the pope. Churches left some buildings as memorials rather than painting over them. Church groups now run reconciliation work: survivors and people who killed, meeting in small groups, sometimes for a long time, telling the truth and slowly learning to live on the same hill. Never again is easy to say. These are people trying to mean it.

Picture terraced hillsides in morning mist, a woman carrying water up a path, a minibus climbing a red-earth road; all of that is Rwanda too. Then, without trying to imagine the violence, hold the survivors, still living with what they saw, and those making peace with neighbors who wronged them. If you pray, pray for Rwanda, for survivors, and for those doing the slow work of reconciliation.
Rwanda. A country of churches where genocide reached inside them, where some believers betrayed and others rescued, and where reconciliation work continues.
Your line: never again, truly. People on the same hill, trying to mean it. Take care until tomorrow.

chat.says: How could churches in Rwanda be part of a genocide? Weren't churches safe places?
options: Some clergy betrayed people while other believers hid them and died; both are true, and churches now work at healing.
Churches stayed neutral: no clergy took any part, and everyone who reached one was kept safe there.
Only foreign missionaries were involved; Rwandan believers themselves had no part in it, either way.
chat.meaning: In some churches people were massacred; some clergy took part, while other believers hid people and some died for it. Churches now run reconciliation work.
